title: Unsafe Rust
summary: Why unsafe exists, the five unsafe superpowers, raw pointers, unsafe functions and the 2024-edition rules, building split_at_mut as a safe abstraction, extern functions and FFI, mutable statics, unsafe traits, unions, undefined behavior, SAFETY comments and Miri.

TRPL 20.1 Using Miri to Check Unsafe Code

blocks.md:
Everything so far was **safe Rust**: the compiler proved your program free of data races, dangling pointers and use-after-free. Its checks are conservative, though. Some correct programs cannot be proven correct by the compiler, and some work (talking to hardware, calling C, building data structures like `Vec`) needs operations the checks cannot reason about.

**`unsafe`** is how you tell the compiler: "for this block, I take responsibility for the rules you cannot check." It does **not** turn off the borrow checker or any other check. It unlocks exactly five extra abilities.

blocks.title: The five unsafe superpowers
rows: call an unsafe function or method
access or modify a mutable static variable

blocks.title: Undefined behavior
blocks.md: *Programming Rust* frames unsafe in terms of **undefined behavior** (UB): things like reading freed memory, creating two `&mut` to the same data, or producing an invalid `bool`. Safe Rust cannot cause UB. Inside `unsafe`, **you** must make sure it cannot happen, because the compiler assumes it never does and optimizes accordingly. A program with UB may seem to work today and break with the next compiler version.

blocks.title: Raw pointers

error[E0133]: dereference of raw pointer is unsafe and requires unsafe function or block
 --> src/main.rs:4:27
  |
4 |     println!("r1 is: {}", *r1);

  = note: raw pointers may be null, dangling or unaligned; they can violate aliasing rules and cause data races: all of these are undefined behavior

blocks.title: Unsafe functions and SAFETY comments
blocks.md:
An `unsafe fn` has requirements (a **contract**) the compiler cannot check. Callers must uphold them, so calling it needs an `unsafe` block. Document the contract in a `# Safety` section of the doc comment, and justify each `unsafe` block with a `// SAFETY:` comment saying why the contract holds there.

Since the 2024 edition, the body of an `unsafe fn` is **not** automatically an unsafe block: unsafe operations inside it still need their own `unsafe { }` (the `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` lint warns otherwise). That keeps each dangerous step visible.

blocks.title: A safe abstraction over unsafe code
blocks.md: Most unsafe code is wrapped inside a **safe function**: the function checks whatever it must, then uses unsafe internally, and callers never see the danger. *The Rust Programming Language*'s example is `split_at_mut`, which splits one mutable slice into two that do not overlap. Written in safe Rust, the borrow checker refuses it:

blocks.output:
error[E0499]: cannot borrow `*values` as mutable more than once at a time
 --> src/main.rs:6:31
  |
1 | fn split_at_mut(values: &mut [i32], mid: usize) -> (&mut [i32], &mut [i32]) {
  |                         - let's call the lifetime of this reference `'1`
...
6 |     (&mut values[..mid], &mut values[mid..])
  |     --------------------------^^^^^^--------
  |     |     |                   |
  |     |     |                   second mutable borrow occurs here
  |     |     first mutable borrow occurs here
  |     returning this value requires that `*values` is borrowed for `'1`
  |
  = help: use `.split_at_mut(position)` to obtain two mutable non-overlapping sub-slices
blocks.explain: We know the two halves do not overlap, but the borrow checker only sees two mutable borrows of the same slice.
The `assert!` is what makes the function safe: without it, a `mid` past the end would create a slice over memory we do not own. A function marked safe must be safe for **every** input.

steps.title: The signature ties lifetimes together
steps.md: Elided lifetimes give both returned slices the lifetime of `values`. While they live, nobody else can touch `v`.

steps.title: The assert checks the input
steps.md: `mid <= len` guarantees both ranges are inside the allocation.

steps.title: The ranges do not overlap
steps.md: `[0, mid)` and `[mid, len)` share no element, so the two `&mut` never alias.

steps.title: The unsafe block is small
steps.md: Only the two `from_raw_parts_mut` calls are unsafe, and the SAFETY comment says why their contract holds. Reviewers can check the reasoning in one place.

blocks.title: extern functions and FFI
blocks.md:
Rust can call functions written in other languages through a **foreign function interface** (FFI). Declare them in an `unsafe extern "C"` block; `"C"` names the **ABI**, the calling convention. Rust cannot check foreign code, so in the 2024 edition the block itself is marked `unsafe`, and each function is either `safe fn` (you vouch that any call is fine) or plain `fn`, whose calls need `unsafe`. Chapter 24 does this in depth.

Going the other way, `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub extern "C" fn call_from_c() { ... }` exports a Rust function with a C name.

blocks.title: Mutable statics
blocks.md: A `static` has one fixed address for the whole program. A `static mut` can be changed, but any thread could do so at any time, so **every access is unsafe**. Since the 2024 edition, even creating a shared reference to one (which `println!` does) is a hard error; read it through a raw pointer instead. In real code prefer atomics (`AtomicU32`) or a `Mutex` in a plain `static`, which need no unsafe at all.

blocks.title: Unsafe traits and unions
blocks.md:
A trait is `unsafe` when implementing it promises something the compiler cannot check. `Send` and `Sync` are the main ones: the compiler implements them automatically, but a type holding raw pointers loses them, and `unsafe impl Send for MyType {}` asserts "I checked this is safe to move across threads".

A **union** is like a struct where all fields share the same memory. Only one field is valid at a time, and Rust cannot know which, so reading a field is unsafe. Unions exist mainly for C interop.

1.0f32 has bits 0x3f800000
null in thread: true

blocks.title: Miri
blocks.md: **Miri** is an interpreter for Rust's intermediate code that detects many kinds of undefined behavior at run time: out-of-bounds access, use after free, invalid aliasing. Install it with `rustup +nightly component add miri` and run `cargo +nightly miri test`. It finds bugs that tests alone miss, but only on code paths your tests execute.

blocks.title: Swapping through raw pointers
blocks.md: Write `fn swap_ends(v: &mut [i32])` that swaps the first and last elements using raw pointers and `std::ptr::swap`. Handle the empty slice safely first (an empty slice has no first element), and add a SAFETY comment explaining why your unsafe block is sound.
hints: `let p = v.as_mut_ptr();` then `p.add(len - 1)` points at the last element.
`std::ptr::swap(a, b)` is an unsafe function taking two `*mut T`.

blocks.title: Safe wrappers over unsafe code
blocks.goal: Write small unsafe blocks behind safe APIs, checking every precondition so callers can never cause undefined behavior.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub fn split_at_mut<T>(v: &mut [T], mid: usize) -> (&mut [T], &mut [T])`: like the lesson, generic. Panic if `mid > v.len()`.
- `pub fn first_last_mut<T>(v: &mut [T]) -> Option<(&mut T, &mut T)>`: mutable references to the first and last element at once; `None` if fewer than **two** elements (with one element they would alias).
- `pub fn read_u32_le(bytes: &[u8], offset: usize) -> Option<u32>`: read 4 bytes at `offset` as a little-endian `u32` with `std::ptr::read_unaligned` (then `u32::from_le`); `None` if out of range. Watch out for `offset + 4` overflowing.
- `pub fn sum_raw(ptr: *const i32, len: usize) -> i32`, an **`unsafe fn`** with a `# Safety` doc section, and a safe `pub fn sum(v: &[i32]) -> i32` that calls it.
hints: `first_last_mut`: `let p = v.as_mut_ptr(); unsafe { Some((&mut *p, &mut *p.add(len - 1))) }` after checking `len >= 2`.
`offset.checked_add(4)` returns `None` on overflow; compare the result with `bytes.len()`.
In `sum_raw`, `std::slice::from_raw_parts(ptr, len)` turns the pointer back into a slice.
blocks.solution_explain: Every safe function checks its inputs before the unsafe block, so no argument can lead to undefined behavior; that is what makes it OK to call them safe. `first_last_mut` refuses a one-element slice because two `&mut` to the same element would alias. `checked_add` closes the overflow hole an `offset + 4 > len` test would leave.

points: unsafe unlocks five things: raw pointer deref, unsafe calls, mutable statics, unsafe traits, union fields.
Inside unsafe you must prevent undefined behavior yourself.
Wrap unsafe in small blocks behind safe functions that validate inputs; document contracts with `# Safety` and `// SAFETY:`.
Prefer atomics and Mutex over static mut; check unsafe code with Miri.

terms.def: A keyword marking code where the programmer, not the compiler, guarantees memory safety.
*const T or *mut T: a pointer with no borrowing or validity guarantees.
An operation the language gives no meaning to, such as reading freed memory; the compiler assumes it never happens.
Foreign function interface: calling code written in another language, or being called from it.
Application binary interface: how functions are called at the machine level, such as "C".
An interpreter that detects undefined behavior while running Rust tests.
